title: Passing on messages
cando: report what people said, asked and wanted

about.text: At work, people often call when the person they want is not there. In this lesson you take messages and pass them on: you report what people said, what they asked and what they wanted. You also read a message slip and a short witness statement, and you take a phone message for a colleague.
goals: Report what someone said: She said that the order was ready.
Report questions and requests: He asked if you were free. She asked me to ring her back.
Read a message slip and a short witness statement.
Write a clear message for a colleague.
Take a phone message and pass it on accurately.

chapters.title: The message at the desk
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you pass on messages. It happens every day at work.
Someone phones, but the person they want is not there. So you take a message, and later you pass it on.
First, you listen to Mei. She works at the front desk of a delivery company. Her colleague Samir comes back from a meeting, and Mei tells him about a phone call.
Listen to how she does it. She does not repeat the caller word for word. She says: He said that the delivery would be late. He asked me to tell you. He wanted to know if you could ring him back.
Listen for the phone phrases too. It was a bad line, so I asked him to speak up. He couldn't reach you. I'll pass it on.

chapters.title: Reporting what people said, asked and wanted
chapters.text:
When you report what someone said, the verb often moves back in time.
The caller says: I'm running late. You report: She said that she was running late.
Is becomes was. Will becomes would. Can becomes could.
Be careful with say and tell. Tell needs a person: she told me. Say does not: she said that. Never say: she said me.
Questions change too. The caller asks: Are you free on Monday? You report: She asked if you were free on Monday. The word order is normal again: if you were free, not were you free.
For instructions and requests, use told or asked, then a person, then to. He told me to wait. She asked me to ring her back.
And for what people want, say: She wants you to call her.

chapters.title: A message slip and a statement
chapters.text:
Next, you read two short documents.
The first is a message slip. Many offices use slips like this. They are called While you were out. A slip shows who called, when they called, and what they want.
The second is a short witness statement. A witness writes down what they saw and heard. Notice how the statement reports people's words: He told me that he had hurt his wrist. I asked him if he wanted an ambulance.
Then you write a message for a colleague. Say who called and when, what they said, and what they want your colleague to do.

chapters.title: Taking a phone message
chapters.text:
Then you take a phone message for a colleague.
Say that your colleague is out, and offer to take a message.
Ask for the caller's name, and ask them to spell it. Write down the number, and read it back to check it.
Ask what the message is, and when is a good time to call back.
Last, pass the message on. Keep it short and accurate: who called, what they said, and what they want.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Finally, you read a story or an article about messages, and how they can change when people pass them on.
Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions.
Notice every time someone reports what another person said, asked or wanted.

warmup.prompt: A colleague is out, and their phone rings. What do you usually do?
choices: answer it and take a message
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Every workplace is different. But if you do take a message, write it down straight away, with the time and the caller's number.

conversation.title: The message at the desk
conversation.setting: Samir works at Northgate Freight, a small delivery company. He comes back from a meeting. Mei, at the front desk, has a message for him.
lines: Mei
Samir, you had a call while you were in your meeting.
Samir
Oh? Who was it?
Mei
Tomasz Nowak, from Westbrook Builders. He said he'd tried your mobile, but he couldn't reach you.
Samir
No, I turned it off for the meeting. What did he say?
Mei
He said that Friday's delivery would be late, because their van had broken down.
Samir
Oh no. Did he say when it would come?
Mei
He said it would probably arrive on Monday morning. And he asked me to tell you not to worry about the extra cost.
Samir
Well, that's something. Did he want anything else?
Mei
Yes, he wanted to know if you could ring him back before four. It was a bad line, so I asked him to speak up and I read his number back to him.
Samir
Thanks. What time did he ring?
Mei
At about half past ten. Oh, and he asked whether you'd got his email.
Samir
I haven't checked yet. Amina's waiting for those boxes. Could you tell her about the delay?
Mei
Of course. I'll pass it on to her straight away.
Samir
Great. Thanks, Mei. That's really clear.

questions.q: Why is Friday's delivery going to be late?
questions.why: Mei says: He said that Friday's delivery would be late, because their van had broken down.

questions.q: What does Tomasz want Samir to do?
questions.why: Mei says: He wanted to know if you could ring him back before four.

questions.q: What does Samir ask Mei to do?
questions.why: Samir says: Amina's waiting for those boxes. Could you tell her about the delay?

phrases.use: Offering to write down a message for someone who is out.

phrases.text: He said that the delivery would be late.
phrases.use: Passing on what someone told you.

phrases.text: He asked me to tell you.
He wanted to know if you could ring him back.
Could you tell her about the delay?
phrases.use: Asking someone to pass on a message.
Promising to give someone the message.

phrases.text: Sorry, it's a bad line. Could you speak up?
phrases.use: When you can't hear the caller well.

items.meaning: To give a message or some information that you received to another person.
items.example: Could you pass on a message to Omar, please?

items.meaning: To contact someone again later, usually with an answer or more information.
items.example: I'm not sure yet, but I'll get back to you this afternoon.

items.meaning: To phone someone again, or to return a call that you missed.
items.example: She's in a meeting. Can she ring you back at three?

items.meaning: To wait for a short time, especially on the phone.
items.example: Hold on a moment, please. I'll see if she's free.

items.meaning: To connect a caller to the person they want to speak to.
items.example: Please hold on. I'll put you through to the sales team.

items.meaning: To speak more loudly, so that people can hear you.
items.example: Sorry, could you speak up? I can't hear you very well.

items.meaning: If you are cut off on the phone, the call suddenly stops before you finish.
items.example: We got cut off in the middle of the conversation.

items.meaning: A call that you did not answer. Your phone shows it to you later.
items.example: I've got three missed calls from the same number.

items.meaning: A service that records a message when you do not answer your phone. The message is also called a voicemail.
items.example: I left a voicemail, but he hasn't called back.

items.meaning: A phone connection that is not clear, so it is hard to hear the other person.
items.example: Sorry, it's a bad line. Can I call you back?

items.meaning: To manage to contact someone, usually by phone.
items.example: I tried all morning, but I couldn't reach her.

items.meaning: To tell someone about something, often in a formal or official way.
items.example: Please inform your manager if you are going to be late.

items.meaning: Using exactly the same words that someone said or wrote.
items.example: He read me the message word for word.

items.meaning: Without meaning to, because of an error.
items.example: I deleted the voicemail by mistake.

items.meaning: To use all of something, so that you have none left.
items.example: We've run out of message slips, so I wrote it on a sticky note.

sound.title: he'd and she'd: had and would made short
sound.explain: When we report what people said, had and would often become 'd. He'd can mean he had or he would. Say it as one short word, not two. Listen, then say each group.
lines: He said he'd tried your mobile.
She said she'd ring back after lunch.
They said they'd send it on Monday.

sayIt.instructions: Say Mei's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Is each part of the message clear and easy to follow?
lines: He said that Friday's delivery would be late, because their van had broken down.
He said it would probably arrive on Monday morning. And he asked me to tell you not to worry about the extra cost.
Yes, he wanted to know if you could ring him back before four. It was a bad line, so I asked him to speak up and I read his number back to him.
Of course. I'll pass it on to her straight away.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Mei is passing on what Tomasz said, asked and wanted.
examples: He said that Friday's delivery would be late.
He asked me to tell you not to worry.
He wanted to know if you could ring him back.
He asked whether you'd got his email.
spot.question: What were Tomasz's real words on the phone? Which verbs changed? Which sentence reports a request, and which ones report questions?
spot.answer: Tomasz said: Friday's delivery will be late. Mei says would, because she is reporting it later. He said: Please tell Samir not to worry. That is a request, so Mei says: He asked me to tell you. He asked: Can Samir ring me back? Has he got my email? Mei reports these questions with if and whether, and the word order is normal: if you could ring him back.

rules.title: Reporting what people said and asked
rule: said (that): 'The van has broken down.' → He said (that) the van had broken down.
told + a person: He told me (that) it was late. Not: He said me.
The verb often moves back: is → was, will → would, can → could.
Yes/no questions: asked if or whether: 'Are you free?' → She asked if I was free.
Wh- questions use normal word order: 'Where is it?' → She asked where it was.
rules.mistake: Not: She asked me where was the file. Say: She asked me where the file was.

rules.title: told me to, asked me to, wants you to
rule: An instruction: told + person + to: 'Wait here.' → He told me to wait here.
A polite request: asked + person + to: 'Could you ring me?' → She asked me to ring her.
Negative: put not before to: He told me not to worry.
What people want: She wants you to call her. He'd like you to sign it.
Questions: wanted to know if / when / where: He wanted to know when you were free.
rules.mistake: Not: She asked me that I call her. Say: She asked me to call her.

practice.q: 'I'm running late.' → She said that she ___ running late.
practice.why: In reported speech, am and is often move back to was.

practice.q: 'The parts will arrive on Monday.' → He said the parts ___ arrive on Monday.
He ___ me that the meeting was cancelled.
practice.why: Told takes a person after it: he told me.

practice.q: She ___ that she'd call back after lunch.
practice.why: Said + that, with no person after it.

practice.q: 'Are you free on Friday?' → He asked ___ I was free on Friday.
practice.why: A yes/no question is reported with if or whether.

practice.q: 'Where is the bill?' → She asked me where ___ .
practice.why: A reported question uses normal word order: the bill was.

practice.q: 'Please call me back.' → She asked me ___ her back.
practice.why: Asked + person + to + verb: she asked me to call her back.

practice.q: 'Don't press that button.' → He told me ___ that button.
practice.why: A negative instruction: told me not to + verb.

practice.q: The caller wanted to know when ___ .
practice.why: A reported question uses normal order, and the verb moves back: you were free.

practice.q: 'Could you sign the form?' → He ___ me to sign the form.
practice.why: A polite request is reported with asked + person + to.

yourTurn.prompt: This morning your colleague Lena left you this voicemail: “Hi, it's Lena. I'm stuck in traffic, so I'll be about twenty minutes late. Can you tell the team to start without me? And is the meeting room free this afternoon?” Pass the message on to your manager in three or four sentences.
yourTurn.model: Lena rang at half past eight. She said that she was stuck in traffic and she'd be about twenty minutes late. She asked me to tell the team to start without her. She also wanted to know if the meeting room was free this afternoon.

text.title: A message slip and a witness statement
text.body:
WHILE YOU WERE OUT
For: Ana Costa, Accounts
Taken by: Mei, front desk
Date: Tuesday 14 March · Time: 9.40 a.m.

Caller: Kwame Mensah
Job title: Office manager, Riverside Dental Clinic
Phone: 0161 496 0732
Reference number: NF-2291

Message: He said that their bill, NF-2291, was wrong. They were charged for 12 boxes, but only 10 arrived. He asked you to send a new bill. He also wanted to know if you could ring him back today.

[ ] Will call again   [x] Please call back   [x] Urgent

Note: He's out of the office from 1 p.m., so you can reach him directly on extension 24 before then. In the meantime, I've asked the warehouse to check the delivery note. Sorry about my handwriting! Mei

- - - - - - - -

WITNESS STATEMENT
Name: Mei Lin · Job title: Receptionist
Place: Reception, Northgate Freight
Date and time: Monday 13 March, about 4.15 p.m.

I was on duty at the front desk. A visitor, Mr Carlos Ruiz, slipped on the wet floor near the door, and I went to help him. He told me that he had hurt his wrist. I asked him if he wanted an ambulance, and he said that he didn't. He asked me to call his wife. The cleaner told me that he had put up a warning sign. As far as I know, the sign was behind the door, so Mr Ruiz couldn't see it. I told Mr Ruiz to sit down, and I got the first aid box. His wife arrived at 4.40 p.m. and took him to the hospital.

Signed: Mei Lin

gist.q: What is the first document for?
gist.a: to pass on a phone message to Ana
gist.why: It is a While you were out slip: a message for Ana Costa from a caller.

gist.q: What is the witness statement about?
gist.a: a visitor who slipped and hurt his wrist
gist.why: Mei writes that a visitor slipped on the wet floor and hurt his wrist.

detail.q: What does Kwame Mensah want Ana to do?
detail.a: send a new bill and ring him back
detail.why: He asked Ana to send a new bill, and he wanted to know if she could ring him back.

detail.q: When is the best time for Ana to ring Kwame?
detail.why: He's out of the office from 1 p.m., so Ana should ring before then.

detail.q: What did Mr Ruiz ask Mei to do?
detail.why: Mei writes: He asked me to call his wife. He said that he didn't want an ambulance.

detail.q: Why couldn't Mr Ruiz see the warning sign?
wrong: He was looking at his phone.
detail.why: Mei writes: As far as I know, the sign was behind the door.

items.meaning: A person who phones you or your office.
items.example: The caller didn't leave a name.

items.meaning: A number that a company gives to an order, a bill or a problem, so that everyone can find it quickly.
items.example: Please have your reference number ready when you call.

items.meaning: The name of someone's job, for example sales manager or receptionist.
items.example: What's her job title? Is she the office manager?

items.meaning: You say this when you think something is true, but you are not completely sure.
items.example: As far as I know, the meeting is still on Thursday.

items.meaning: Working at a particular time, especially in a job with shifts.
items.example: Two security guards are on duty every night.

items.meaning: One of the phone numbers inside a company. You call the main number, then the extension.
items.example: You can reach me on extension 214.

items.meaning: Without going through another person or place.
items.example: Please call me directly on my mobile.

items.meaning: Not at your workplace, for example because you are at a meeting somewhere else, travelling or on holiday.
items.example: I'm out of the office until Monday.

items.meaning: The way a person writes with a pen.
items.example: I can't read this note. Whose handwriting is it?

items.meaning: In the time between now and something that will happen later.
items.example: The engineer is coming at two. In the meantime, please use the other printer.

model.title: A message for a colleague
model.body:
To: Lena
From: Tomasz
Time: 11.15 a.m., Wednesday

Priya Nair from Harbour Print rang. She said that your posters would be ready on Thursday, not Wednesday, because their machine had broken down. She asked you to check the colours in the file she sent yesterday. She also wanted to know if you could call her back before 3 p.m. Her number is 0161 496 0415, extension 12. In the meantime, she's going to print one test copy for you.

write.task: You took a phone message for a colleague. Write the message you were given, like the model. Say who called and when, what they said, what they asked, and what they want your colleague to do. It can be real or made up.
checklist: I said who called, and when.
I reported what they said with said that or told me that.
I reported a question or a request: asked if …, asked you to …
I wrote a phone number and the best time to call back.

card.title: Take a phone message
card.situation: You work at Northgate Freight. Your colleague Priya is at the dentist until two o'clock. Her phone rings, and you answer it.
card.goal: Take a message: the caller's name, number and message. Check the details. Then pass the message on to Priya, accurately.

phrases: Hello, Priya Shah's phone. Can I help you?
I'm afraid she's out of the office until two. Can I take a message?
Could you spell your name, please?
Let me read that back to you.
I'll make sure she gets the message.
Priya, … rang. She said that … . She asked you to …
prepare.notes: Before you start, draw a small message slip: Caller, Phone, Time, Message, Call back? Fill it in while you listen. Then use it to pass the message on.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher phones and asks for Priya. Take a message and check the details. Then tell the class what the caller said, asked and wanted. Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You are a customer called Mr Hassan. You phone my office and ask for my colleague Priya, but she is out. Leave a message with your name, your phone number, one piece of news and one request. When I have taken the message, ask me to read it back to you. Correct me if I get something wrong. Use simple English.

model.title: The call, and passing it on
lines: You
Hello, Priya Shah's phone. Can I help you?
Caller
Hello. Could I speak to Priya, please?
You
I'm afraid she's out of the office until two. Can I take a message?
Caller
Yes, please. It's Amina Yusuf, from Greenway Foods.
You
Could you spell your family name, please?
Caller
Y-U-S-U-F. Can you tell her that the order is ready, but our van can't deliver it until Friday? And could she ring me back today?
You
Of course. What's the best number to reach you on?
Caller
You
Let me read that back: 0161 496 0587. The order is ready, but you can't deliver it until Friday, and you'd like Priya to ring you back today.
Caller
That's right. Thanks very much.
You
Priya, Amina Yusuf from Greenway Foods rang at half past eleven.
Priya
Oh, thanks. What did she say?
You
She said that the order was ready, but they couldn't deliver it until Friday. She asked you to ring her back today. Her number's on your desk.
Priya
Great, that's really clear. Thanks.
compare: Did you offer to take a message?
Did you check the spelling of the name and read the number back?
Did you pass on the news with said that, and the request with asked you to?
Was your message short and accurate?

canDo: I can report what someone said: She said that the order was ready.
I can report questions and requests: He asked if …, She asked me to …
I can read a message slip and a short witness statement.
I can write a clear message for a colleague.
I can take a phone message and pass it on accurately.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who is passing on a message, and who is it for? What do you think goes wrong?
reading.talk: Did the message arrive safely in the story? Think of a time when a message changed as people passed it on. Write three or four sentences, or tell Wehel about it.

quiz.q: 'I'll call you tomorrow.' → She said that she ___ call me the next day.
quiz.why: Will moves back to would in reported speech.

quiz.q: He ___ me that the parcel had arrived.
quiz.why: Told takes a person after it: he told me.

quiz.q: 'Is the lift working?' → She asked ___ the lift was working.
quiz.why: A yes/no question is reported with if or whether.

quiz.q: 'Please sign here.' → The driver asked me ___ there.
Sorry, I can't hear you. Could you speak ___ ?
quiz.why: Speak up means speak more loudly.

quiz.q: I'm afraid she's in a meeting. Can I take a ___ ?
quiz.why: Can I take a message? means: I can pass it on to her.

quiz.q: Call the main number, then ask for ___ 214.
quiz.why: An extension is a phone number inside a company.

quiz.q: When I got to the station, the train ___ .
quiz.why: The past perfect shows the earlier of two past actions.

quiz.q: I'll call you as soon as I ___ home.
quiz.why: After as soon as, use the present to talk about the future.

quiz.q: The form must ___ by your manager.
quiz.why: The passive after must: must be + past participle.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the conversation at the desk in pairs. Then change the caller, the news and the request, and pass the new message on.
Day 2: a message chain. Whisper a short message to the first learner. Each learner reports it to the next with said that, asked me to or wanted to know. Compare the last version with the first.
Day 3: the task. You phone each learner and ask for a colleague who is out. They take a message, read the details back, then pass it on to the class.
Day 4: talk about the book and answer questions. Then two learners read their messages aloud, and the class checks what was said, asked and wanted.
